paras: The lynching of Joe Drake took place on the night of December 18, 1903, when a mob of about 100 men took Drake, a young Black prisoner, from the Lauderdale County jail at Ripley, Tennessee, and hanged him to a tree near the jail. Drake had been arrested on the accusation of killing Chester Conner, a young white man, at Ashport that day. The mob shot the body many times, and white papers from Tennessee to Washington state carried the news as a murder avenged.

Conner was described as "a prominent young white man" of Ashport, in Lauderdale County. The Paducah Sun's Ripley report stated flatly that Drake "shot and instantly killed" him, while other dispatches said only that Drake had been "arrested for the killing". The reports differ on the hour of the killing: a Memphis dispatch of December 18 placed it "this morning," the Paducah Sun "last night," and the St. Louis Republic "yesterday."

Ripley had seen a lynching at the same spot before. According to the Paducah Sun, Lewis Rice, "colored," had been hanged by a mob from the same limb in March 1900; the Republic called him Louis Rice and dated it "three years ago."

At about 10:30 that night a mob of about 100 men came to the jail, its leaders masked. They told the jailer, Andrew Crockett, that they wanted Drake, overpowered him and took his keys; the Republic's correspondent added that Crockett was thrown to the floor and held down until the prisoner was secured. Crockett, the Republic said, had been taken by surprise, believing "that the idea of lynching the negro had been abandoned."

The mob dragged Drake from his cell to a tree, which the Paducah Sun placed 200 yards from the jail near an old gin site and the Republic about 150 yards away. A Mississippi weekly that printed the Republic's text located the spot "in a hollow west of the Western Hotel." Within five minutes, by the Paducah Sun's account, Drake was hanging from the limb. After he was thought dead the mob fired "something like fifty shots" into the body and dispersed.
The Republic reported that the work was done quietly: "Not a word was spoken until the street was reached." No one in the mob was named.
Conner's funeral was held on the afternoon of December 19. No report of an inquest, arrest, grand jury inquiry or Black community response appears in the coverage, nor any account of Drake's burial.

The first reports went out on December 18 and 19 in two forms: a dispatch from the Memphis Commercial Appeal's Ripley correspondent and a fuller Ripley report printed by the Paducah Sun. The Indianapolis Journal headed the Memphis version "NEGRO LYNCHED FOR KILLING A WHITE MAN," and the Paducah Sun ran its account under "MURDER IS AVENGED," describing the mob's "very determined, though orderly, manner." A St. Louis Republic special of December 20 added the jailer's surprise, the fifty shots and the funeral, under the deck "Tennessee Mob Avenges Death of White Man."

Short telegrams ran the same day in Connecticut, Montana, Idaho and Washington, where the Lewiston and Walla Walla papers called the victim "a negro murderer." The New York Sun reprinted the Republic text as "Young Negro Murderer Taken From Jail and Hanged." Over the next two weeks Mississippi weeklies printed the story under "Lynching at Ripley, Tenn.," giving the name as Joe Brack, and the Lawrence Democrat in Tennessee repeated the Paducah account on December 25. One-sentence items still appeared in New Jersey and South Carolina papers as late as January 6, 1904.
None of these papers questioned Drake's guilt or criticized the mob. No Black-press report naming Drake or the Ripley lynching was found.

The victim's name appeared as Joe Drake in the Ripley specials and the Tennessee weekly, as Joe or Joseph Brake in the Memphis wire, and as Joe Brack in the Mississippi wire; all describe a single man.

accounts.label: Commercial Appeal dispatch (via Memphis)
accounts.gist: A mob of about one hundred men took 'Joe Brake' from the county jail on the night of Dec. 18 and hanged him near by; the leaders were masked and the body was riddled with bullets before being cut down.

accounts.label: Ripley dispatch (Paducah Sun version)
accounts.gist: Masked leaders entered the jail at 10:30 'in a very determined, though orderly, manner', overpowered jailer Andrew Crockett, and within five minutes hanged Drake 200 yards away near an old gin site, on the limb used in the 1900 lynching of Lewis Rice; the body was shot full of holes.

accounts.label: Republic special from Ripley
accounts.gist: About 100 men overpowered the jailer, threw him to the floor, dragged Drake about 150 yards and hanged him, then fired some fifty shots into the body; the jailer had believed the lynching idea abandoned.

framing.detail: The Paducah Sun headed its report 'MURDER IS AVENGED' and stated as fact that Drake 'shot and instantly killed' Conner, describing the mob as 'very determined, though orderly'.
The St. Louis Republic headlined 'NEGRO LYNCHED FOR MURDER. Tennessee Mob Avenges Death of White Man.' and stressed that 'Everything was accomplished in a quiet manner.'
Distant papers ran two-line telegrams under 'Negro Lynched' or 'Negro Murderer Lynched', calling the victim 'a negro murderer'.
Mississippi weeklies carried a Dec. 20 wire, 'Lynching at Ripley, Tenn.', that said only that he had been 'arrested for the killing' of 'a prominent young white man'.
